standard.title: Language features construct meaning
standard.description: recognise that target language components and/or characters and features of language are used to construct meaning
standard.prior_knowledge: Students have noticed features of the target language writing system and compared them with English (AC9LCHF02). They can copy familiar words with attention to script conventions (AC9LCH2C05). They have not yet examined how components, characters or grammatical features of the target language systematically construct meaning — how word-building elements combine, how word order operates, or how grammatical categories function.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students recognise that components, characters and grammatical features of the target language are used to construct meaning — including how characters or words are built, how word order works, and how grammatical features such as adjectives, prepositions, question words and measure words operate in context.

nodes.label: How characters or words are built
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify how the target language builds characters or words from components, recognising that elements combine to construct meaning.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two examples of how components or elements combine in the target language to build a word or character, and explain the connection to meaning.
nodes.typical_width: Explore how characters or words are constructed from components or morphemes; make connections between shared components and related meanings; understand that words may be made up of multiple meaningful units; create or copy characters and words with attention to how components contribute to the whole.
wider: Investigate a group of words or characters sharing a common component and identify the semantic or phonetic connection — explain the pattern to a peer
Compare how words are built in the target language with how compound words or word parts work in English — identify similarities and differences in word construction logic
nodes.hinge_reason: Understanding how characters or words are built is the prerequisite for all subsequent work with vocabulary, reading and writing in the target language. Students who treat each word as an arbitrary string cannot use component knowledge to infer meaning, extend vocabulary, or understand the logic of the writing system.

response_modes.reason: Word and character construction is not transparent — students need explicit instruction on how components combine and why. Guided analysis of component patterns, with discussion of the semantic or phonetic logic, builds the systematic knowledge that allows students to approach unfamiliar words strategically.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The logic of how the target language constructs meaning through components or morphemes is often revelatory for background learners who know words without having examined how they work. Width investment here builds metalinguistic awareness that transfers to both reading comprehension and vocabulary extension.
success_criteria: Identifies at least two examples of component combination in the target language with an explanation of how the components contribute to meaning
Can make at least one connection between a shared component and related meaning across two or more words

nodes.label: Word order and basic grammatical structures
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify basic word order patterns in the target language and recognise how grammatical structures — adjectives, prepositions, question words, measure words — function in context.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify the basic subject-verb-object word order in at least two target language sentences and correctly use at least one grammatical feature (adjective, preposition, or question word) in a modelled sentence.
nodes.typical_width: Recognise and apply basic word order rules; use common adjectives to describe people and objects; use prepositions for location; use question words in familiar contexts; use measure words with numbers in modelled sentences; notice similarities and differences between word order in the target language and English.
wider: Compare the placement of adjectives, adverbs or question words in the target language with English — identify where they appear in the same position and where they differ
Create a set of target language sentences demonstrating different grammatical features — annotate each sentence to show how each part contributes to meaning

response_modes.reason: Grammatical structures at Y1-2 are best encountered in varied contexts — reading, listening, play and production — rather than through isolated exercises. Students need to recognise and use structures across different sentence types and topics before the patterns become reliable.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Background learners often use these structures correctly in speech without being able to explain them. Width investment in making grammatical patterns explicit — analysing what they already do — builds metalinguistic awareness that strengthens both accuracy and ability to explain the language to others.
success_criteria: Identifies subject-verb-object word order in at least two target language sentences
Correctly uses at least one grammatical feature (adjective, preposition, question word, or measure word) in a modelled sentence

nodes.label: Punctuation conventions
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can identify similarities and differences between punctuation conventions in the target language and English, and use target language punctuation correctly in short texts.
nodes.minimum_width: Identify at least two punctuation marks in the target language, describe whether they are the same as or different from English equivalents, and use them correctly in a short text.
nodes.typical_width: Notice and discuss similarities and differences between target language and English punctuation conventions; use correct punctuation in created texts; understand the function of key punctuation marks in the target language.
wider: Compare a target language and English text of the same type — identify every punctuation difference and discuss what each reveals about the two writing systems
Create a bilingual mini-guide to punctuation conventions, explaining to a peer what is the same and what is different

response_modes.reason: Punctuation conventions integrate character/word knowledge (node 1) and grammatical structure awareness (node 2) into the full writing system. The teaching investment is in contextualised writing tasks that require correct punctuation for meaning — not isolated punctuation exercises.

success_criteria: Identifies at least two target language punctuation marks and describes how they compare with English
Uses correct punctuation in at least one short created text
